title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: At eight o'clock, Kutuzov rode toward Pratzen at the head of the fourth column — Miloradovich's — which was supposed to replace the columns of Przhebyshevsky and Langeron, both of which had already descended into the valley. He greeted the soldiers of the lead regiment and gave the order to march, signaling that he intended to lead this column himself. When they reached the village of Pratzen, he halted. Prince Andrei rode behind, lost among the enormous crowd that made up the commander in chief's retinue. He was in a state of suppressed excitement and agitation, though outwardly calm — the way a person gets when a long-anticipated moment is finally at hand. He was firmly convinced that this would be his Toulon, his bridge of Arcole. He didn't know exactly how it would happen, but he was certain it would. He knew the terrain and the positions of the troops as well as anyone in the army could. His own strategic plan, now clearly impossible to carry out, had been set aside. Instead, working within Weyrother's plan, Prince Andrei considered possible developments and formed new projects that might call for his quick thinking and decisive action.

Down to the left, through the mist, the crackle of musket fire from unseen forces could be heard. That was where Prince Andrei expected the fighting to intensify. "That's where the difficulties will come," he thought, "and that's where I'll be sent with a brigade or a division. There, with the standard in my hand, I'll charge forward and break through whatever stands in my way."
He couldn't look calmly at the regimental standards as the battalions passed by. Each time he saw one, he kept thinking: "That might be the very standard I'll carry when I lead the army."

By morning, all that remained of the night's fog on the heights was a thin frost turning to dew, but down in the valleys it still lay like a sea of white milk. Nothing was visible in the valley to the left, where the troops had descended and where the gunfire was coming from. Above the heights stretched a dark, clear sky, and to the right hung the vast disk of the sun. In the distance, on the far shore of that misty sea, some wooded hills were just barely visible — the enemy was probably there, since something could be made out moving. To the right, the Guards were entering the mist with the sound of hooves and wheels, and now and then a glint of bayonets; to the left, beyond the village, similar masses of cavalry appeared and vanished into the white sea. In front and behind, infantry moved forward. The commander in chief stood at the edge of the village, watching the troops pass. That morning, Kutuzov seemed worn out and irritable. The infantry marching past him suddenly came to a halt without any order being given, apparently blocked by something ahead.

"Order them to form battalion columns and go around the village!" he said angrily to a general who had ridden up. "Don't you understand, your excellency, my dear sir, that you can't march through narrow village streets when we're advancing against the enemy?"
"I was planning to re-form them on the other side of the village, your excellency," the general replied.
Kutuzov gave a bitter laugh.
"That'll work out wonderfully — deploying in full view of the enemy! Just wonderful!"
"The enemy is still far away, your excellency. According to the battle plan —"
"The battle plan!" Kutuzov snapped bitterly. "Who told you that? Do as you're ordered."
"Yes, sir."
"My dear fellow," Nesvitsky whispered to Prince Andrei, "the old man is in a foul mood."
An Austrian officer in a white uniform with green plumes on his hat galloped up to Kutuzov and asked, on behalf of the Emperor, whether the fourth column had advanced into action.

Kutuzov turned away without answering, and his gaze happened to fall on Prince Andrei standing beside him. When he saw him, Kutuzov's bitter, caustic expression softened, as if acknowledging that none of this was his adjutant's fault. Still ignoring the Austrian, he addressed Bolkonsky.
"Go, my dear fellow, and see whether the third division has passed the village. Tell them to stop and wait for my orders."
Prince Andrei had barely started when Kutuzov stopped him.
"And find out if they've posted sharpshooters," he added. "What are they doing? What are they doing?" he muttered to himself, still not answering the Austrian.
Prince Andrei galloped off to carry out the order.

Riding past the advancing battalions, he stopped the third division and confirmed that there were indeed no sharpshooters deployed ahead of the columns. The colonel leading the regiment was shocked by the commander in chief's order to send out skirmishers. He had been certain there were other troops in front of him and that the enemy must be at least six miles away. In truth, nothing was visible ahead except a barren slope hidden by thick mist. After issuing orders in the commander in chief's name to correct this oversight, Prince Andrei galloped back. Kutuzov was still in the same place, his heavy body sagging wearily in the saddle, yawning with closed eyes. The troops had stopped and now stood with the butts of their muskets resting on the ground.
"All right, all right!" he said to Prince Andrei, then turned to a general who, watch in hand, was insisting it was time to move since all the left-flank columns had already gone down.
"Plenty of time, your excellency," Kutuzov muttered through a yawn. "Plenty of time," he repeated.

Just then, from somewhere behind Kutuzov, came the sound of regiments cheering, and the wave of salutes rolled rapidly closer along the whole extended line of advancing Russian columns. Clearly, whoever they were greeting was riding quickly. When the soldiers in the regiment nearest Kutuzov began to shout, he moved off to the side a little and looked back with a frown. A squadron-like group of horsemen in various uniforms came galloping along the road from Pratzen. Two of them rode ahead, side by side, at full gallop. One wore a black uniform with white plumes and rode a short-tailed chestnut horse; the other wore white and rode a black horse. These were the two Emperors, followed by their entourages. Kutuzov, putting on the manner of a grizzled old soldier at the front, called out "Attention!" and rode up to the Emperors with a salute. His entire appearance and demeanor were suddenly transformed. He adopted the air of a subordinate who obeys without question. With a show of deference that clearly struck Alexander as excessive, he rode up and saluted.

This unpleasant impression merely passed across the young and joyful face of the Emperor like a wisp of haze drifting over a clear sky, and was gone. After his illness, he looked somewhat thinner than he had on the field of Olmutz, where Bolkonsky had first seen him abroad. But there was still the same captivating blend of majesty and gentleness in his fine gray eyes, and on his delicate lips the same ability to shift expression, with the same prevailing look of warmhearted, innocent youth.

At the Olmutz review, he had seemed more majestic; here he seemed brighter and more full of energy. He was slightly flushed from galloping two miles, and as he reined in his horse, he sighed with relief and looked around at his companions — all of them as young and animated as himself. Czartoryski, Novosiltsev, Prince Volkonsky, Strogonov, and the rest — all richly dressed, cheerful young men on splendid, well-groomed, barely warm horses — had stopped behind the Emperor, exchanging remarks and smiling. Emperor Francis, a rosy, long-faced young man, sat very straight on his handsome black horse, looking about in a leisurely and preoccupied way. He beckoned to one of his white-uniformed adjutants and asked some question. "He's probably asking what time they set out," thought Prince Andrei, watching this old acquaintance with a smile he couldn't suppress as he recalled his reception at Brunn. Among the two Emperors' retinues were the finest young orderly officers from the Guard and line regiments, both Russian and Austrian. Mixed in among them were grooms leading the Tsar's beautiful reserve horses draped in embroidered cloths.

The way a gust of fresh air from the fields sweeps into a stuffy room when a window is opened — that was how a rush of youthfulness, energy, and confidence reached Kutuzov's gloomy staff as all these brilliant young men came galloping up.
"Why haven't you started, Mikhail Ilarionovich?" Emperor Alexander asked Kutuzov quickly, at the same time casting a courteous glance at Emperor Francis.
"I'm waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov answered, bowing forward respectfully.
The Emperor frowned slightly and leaned his ear forward as if he hadn't quite heard.
"Waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov repeated. (Prince Andrei noticed that Kutuzov's upper lip twitched unnaturally as he said the word "waiting.") "Not all the columns have formed up yet, Your Majesty."
The Tsar heard but clearly didn't like the reply. He shrugged his somewhat rounded shoulders and glanced at Novosiltsev, who stood nearby, as if to complain about Kutuzov.

"You know, Mikhail Ilarionovich, we're not on the parade ground, where the review doesn't begin until all the troops are assembled," the Tsar said with another glance at Emperor Francis, as if inviting him — if not to join in — at least to listen. But Emperor Francis continued to look around and didn't seem to be listening.

"That is exactly why I have not begun, sire," Kutuzov said in a loud, clear voice, evidently making sure he would not go unheard, and again something in his face twitched. "That is exactly why I have not begun, sire — because we are not on parade and not on the Empress's Field." He spoke clearly and distinctly.
Everyone in the Emperor's retinue exchanged quick glances of displeasure and reproach. "Old as he may be, he shouldn't — he absolutely shouldn't — speak like that," their looks seemed to say.

The Tsar stared intently at Kutuzov's face, waiting for him to say something more. But Kutuzov, with his head respectfully bowed, appeared to be waiting as well. The silence stretched on for about a minute.
"However, if you command it, Your Majesty," Kutuzov said at last, raising his head and resuming his former tone — that of a dull, unquestioning, obedient general.
He nudged his horse forward and, calling over Miloradovich, the column commander, gave him the order to advance.
The troops began moving again, and two battalions of the Novgorod regiment and one of the Apsheron regiment marched past the Emperor.

As the Apsheron battalion went by, the red-faced Miloradovich — without his greatcoat, medals pinned to his chest, and a huge plume in his cocked hat worn sideways with corners pointing front and back — galloped energetically forward and reined in his horse before the Emperor with a dashing salute.
"God be with you, General!" said the Emperor.
[Speaking in French] "Indeed, sire, we shall do everything in our power, sire," he answered cheerfully, though his poor French drew ironic smiles from the gentlemen in the Tsar's entourage.
Footnote: "Indeed, Sire, we shall do everything it is possible to do, Sire."

Miloradovich wheeled his horse sharply and positioned himself just behind the Emperor. The Apsheron soldiers, energized by the Tsar's presence, marched past the Emperors and their suites at a bold, brisk pace, keeping perfect step.

"Lads!" Miloradovich shouted in a loud, confident, and cheerful voice — so carried away by the sound of gunfire, the prospect of battle, and the sight of the gallant Apsherons (his old comrades from Suvorov's campaigns, now marching so splendidly past the Emperors) that he forgot the sovereigns were right there. "Lads, it's not the first village you've had to take!" he cried.
"Glad to do our best!" the soldiers shouted back.

The Emperor's horse startled at the sudden cry. This was the same horse that had carried the sovereign through reviews in Russia, and it carried him here too on the field of Austerlitz, bearing the absent-minded kicks of his left foot and pricking its ears at the sound of gunfire — just as it had done on the Empress's Field — without understanding the meaning of the shots, or the proximity of Emperor Francis's black horse, or anything that was being said, thought, and felt by its rider that day.
The Emperor turned with a smile to one of his attendants and said something, pointing at the brave Apsherons.
